question.knowledge_point: Computing Expressions Involving Second-Order Partial Derivatives
question.worked_solution:
To find ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({g}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{2}{2x-y}) \\  & =-\frac{4}{(2x-y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({g}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\frac{1}{2x-y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(2x-y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we evaluate ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ and ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(1,-1) & =-\frac{4}{(2(1)-(-1))^{2}}=-\frac{4}{9} \\ {g}_{yy}(1,-1) & =-\frac{1}{(2(1)-(-1))^{2}}=-\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
{g}_{xx}(1,-1)+{g}_{yy}(1,-1)=-\frac{4}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=-\frac{5}{9}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing Expressions Involving Second-Order Partial Derivatives
question.worked_solution:
To find ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})) \\  & =x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2y)) \\  & =2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})) \\  & =-y(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot 2x) \\  & =2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y)+{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})+2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =4xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we find ${f}_{yyx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{yy}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yyx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =-2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\cdot y \\  & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡xyz) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\cdot yz \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\cdot (-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\cdot (2z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}z(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz))\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ) & =-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \pi \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
question.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=e.$ Given that the point $P(e,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{{e}^{y}}{x}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=e.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(e,2,3)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(e,2).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(e,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(e,2) & =2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\frac{{e}^{2}}{e}=4-e\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=2 \\ z=-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(2,0,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,0,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(2,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,0) & ={e}^{(0)}+2(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =1+4 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(2,0)}(x-2) \\ z-4 & =5(x-2) \\ z & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,0,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3{e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|xy|$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,1) & =3{e}^{-1+1}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(-1)\cdot 1| \\  & =3\cdot 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,1) & ={f}_{x}(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\ z-(-1) & =3(x+1) \\ z+1 & =3x+3 \\ z & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,1,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3x+2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-3\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-3⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-3⟩=⟨1,0,3⟩$ is also parallel to it.

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Row Operations Required To Find the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
question.problem:
The inverse of the matrix $A$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to each step?

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write down $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${A}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{A}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix Calculated Using Row Operations
question.problem:
The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${A}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 &  &  \\ 0 & 1 &  & \end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write down $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${A}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{A}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-3xy+2{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =8x-3y+0+0 \\  & =8x-3y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-3xy+2{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =0-3x+4y+1 \\  & =4y-3x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & ={h}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{h}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =(8x-3y)\text{ }i+(4y-3x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇h(2,3) & =(8\cdot 2-3\cdot 3)\text{ }i+(4\cdot 3-3\cdot 2+1)\text{ }j \\  & =7\text{ }i+7\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & =y{x}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,i+({x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1})j+{y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k.\end{aligned}
$$
